title: Photography direction for an architecture studio
excerpt: Direct photographs so they show built work and the constraint that shaped it. A fullscreen render with no words is a mood. The picture has to argue.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf, objects chosen and placed so the frame makes one clear point.
caption: A shelf edited until the arrangement argues. Project photographs need the same edit. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first photograph on the site show?
faqs.answer: Built work, with the constraint named in the caption or in the frame itself. A finished room, a facade in ordinary light, or a detail that proves the decision. A fullscreen render with no project name teaches the visitor nothing they can hire.

faqs.question: How do we brief a photographer?
faqs.answer: Give them the decision in one sentence before the shoot day. Ask for the approach, the hard moment, the resulting room, and one joint or opening that would have been easy to get wrong. Reject frames that could belong to any practice with the same sky.

faqs.question: Should renders be on the site at all?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the project is not built and you label them as drawings or visualizations. Put them after the best built work you have. An unlabeled cinematic image in the first screen asks a careful client to guess whether the building exists.

markdown:
Direct architecture studio website photography so the pictures show built work, with the constraint named. A client judging taste before competence will decide from the frames before they decide from the copy. A fullscreen render with no words fails them. The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline.

Choose what the frame has to prove, then shoot or select for that proof. Light, crop, and sequence come after the sentence you need the picture to support.

## The picture has a job

Every lead image needs a job you can say aloud. Show the stair that fits the only wall the planner allowed. Show the old front room that had to stay. Show the courtyard that replaced a second storey the budget could not carry. If you cannot say the job, the image is decoration, however well it is printed.

Write the job before the shoot, or before you select from an archive. A photographer can chase light all afternoon and still miss the party wall. Direction is the sentence. The camera is how you keep it.

Put the project name and the constraint where they can be read with the image. Type in the page, not type burned into the file. A reader should not need a click to learn what they are seeing. "House on a lane" plus "single retaining wall" is the minimum. The long account can wait for the project page.

Reject the habit of a fullscreen opening with no words at all. It looks confident in a design review. On a client’s phone it is a pause with no facts. They cannot tell if the building is yours, if it is built, or if it resembles their problem. Taste without a label is how practices become interchangeable.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi project, is a reminder that pictures can carry a point of view when they are chosen, not merely collected. An architecture office has a stricter test. The point of view has to be a built decision. A beautiful object on a shelf is not yet a house.

## Built work, labeled honestly

Lead the site with photographs of things that exist. Ordinary daylight is often more trustworthy than a dusk shot with every interior lamp on. Clients live in their houses at 8 in the morning. Show a room that still makes sense then.

If a project is unbuilt, label the image as a visualization or a model photograph. Place it after at least one built example, even a small one. A young practice with a single finished kitchen should lead with that kitchen. The render of the dream house can follow, named as a render. Thin and true is a position. Cinematic and ambiguous is a risk.

Include people when they explain scale or use. A figure at the table tells you the room is for eating, not only for photographing. Do not stage a lifestyle campaign that hides the architecture. The client is hiring the building, not a wardrobe.

Show age and use if the project has been occupied. A scuff, a real chair, a plant that is slightly too big. Sterile rooms read as sets. Sets are what a fullscreen render already threatened. The built photograph should feel occupied or ready to be occupied, not sealed.

Weather and season can stay in the frame when they are part of the constraint. A house designed for a hot western aspect should not be shown only in soft cloud. If you only have the soft-cloud day, say so in the caption rather than implying the light is always kind.

## What to refuse

Make a short refuse list and keep it next to the selects. It will save you from your own taste.

- A fullscreen render with no project name, no place, and no constraint.
- A skyline, a drone shot of a city, or a material sample that is not from the job.
- Frames that crop the building into an abstract so the desktop composition looks bold.
- Duplicate angles that differ only by a cloud.
- Any image you cannot caption with a decision.

The refuse list is also for the office’s favorite image. Someone will love the twilight hero. Ask whether a stranger can retell the project from it. If the answer is no, it can live lower on the page, or not on the page.

Do not accept a photographer’s sequence unchanged if it was edited for a magazine feature with a different argument. Magazine sequence is often atmosphere, then detail, then plan. Your site sequence is constraint, decision, result. Reorder the folder. You are allowed to leave strong frames out.

Stock photography of architecture is the clearest miss. A client judging taste will feel the stock even when they cannot name it. If you do not have the photograph yet, use a drawing you can explain, or wait. A gap is more honest than a rented tower.

## A brief you can hand over

A one-page brief is enough. Give the photographer the decision sentence, the rooms that matter, the hour you care about, and what you will not shoot. Mention access, occupied clients, and anything that must not be shown. Privacy is part of direction. A beautiful child’s bedroom that the family did not agree to publish is not a win.

Ask for a contact sheet, not a finished grade, at the first pass. Select for the argument. Then grade. If you grade first, you will keep images because the color is flattering.

Agree the crop for the site, not only for a print. Vertical frames for the phone, a stable horizon, and enough context that the building is recognizable at a small size. A crop that needs a 27-inch monitor to make sense will fail the visit that actually happens.

Pay for the usage you need, and keep the agreement where the office can find it. The client portal on a Hanabi project is one place brand files and notes can live after delivery. The photographs are part of that set. A site that depends on a folder in one person’s inbox will lose the best frame at the worst time.

Write captions the day you select, while the decision is fresh. Future you will not remember which wall was the party wall. The caption is the argument surviving the shoot.

## Sequence and the words beside the frame

On the homepage, three projects with one image each, plus a caption, beat a carousel of twelve. Carousels hide the second and third arguments. A client who does not click still needs to see range of judgment, not range of filters.

On the project page, follow the sentence. Approach, so they know the street. The hard condition. The move. The room. A detail. Stop before you repeat yourself. Six to ten images is often the whole case. More is a portfolio inside the portfolio.

[The W3C’s WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats images as content that people need another way to perceive. Alt text should say what is in the frame: the room, the opening, the old wall against the new stair. Do not stuff a slogan into the alt. Do not leave it empty because the caption is nearby and you hope that is enough for every tool. Write the alt as the fact. Write the caption as the decision.

Keep captions in HTML text. Overlay text inside the photograph cannot be translated, resized, or read reliably. It also locks you into a crop. When the sentence improves, you should change the sentence without re-exporting the file.

## Weight, and the first paint

Large architecture files are the usual reason a site feels slow. The hero is often the largest element on the screen. [web.dev’s Web Vitals guidance](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) treats Largest Contentful Paint as the loading measure, and a good experience means that paint happens within 2.5 seconds. A 12-megabyte dusk shot misses that on the phone the client is holding.

Export for the size you display. A hero can be sharp without being a print file. Use modern formats your stack already supports, and give the page the image dimensions so the layout does not jump when the photograph arrives. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less for a good experience. A caption that shoves itself down after the image loads is the picture damaging the argument.

Art direction can include a smaller crop for small screens, so the building stays in frame. That is a design choice and a performance choice. Hanabi builds these sites in Next.js, with images treated as part of the page rather than as an afterthought. The direction document should name the crop and the maximum weight, or the build will guess.

Look at the page on a mid-range phone over a normal connection before you sign off the selects. If the first building appears late, you have directed a print, not a website.

If you want a partner to hold the sentence, the crop, and the page together, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring two projects: one whose photographs already argue, and one that is only a mood. The useful work is telling them apart, then building a site that can keep the captions editable.

## The phone will recrop your hero

Desktop will flatter a wide elevation. The phone will cut it. If the constraint sits in the part of the frame that gets sliced, the direction is unfinished. The next pass is to design the visit as a phone visit: first screen, caption, and a way to start a project conversation, with the building still recognizable.

That pass is [the mobile visit for an architecture studio](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-an-architecture-studio). Shoot and select as if that screen is the real one. It usually is.
